Tamil Nadu has consistently demonstrated a strong commitment to maternal and child healthcare and has achieved remarkable progress in “Ensuring Healthy Mothers and Healthy Newborns” through sustained investments in public health infrastructure, skilled human resources, and comprehensive maternal and child welfare programmes.

2. The State has accorded high priority to maternal healthcare and has implemented several initiatives aimed at providing financial assistance to pregnant women, free delivery and newborn care services, emergency obstetric care, nutritional support, birth preparedness, and digital tracking of beneficiaries. These initiatives supported by a strong network of healthcare institutions and skilled healthcare personnel, have contributed significantly to improving maternal and neonatal health outcomes in the State.

3. Every year, the State records approximately 7.8 lakh deliveries, with institutional deliveries constituting 99.9% of all births as per NFHS-6. Among this, Government health facilities contribute nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries (53%) which reflect the central role of the public health system in providing maternal and newborn healthcare services. Among the Government institutional deliveries, 90% are conducted in 130 Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric and New-born Care (CEmONC) centres.

4. The accessibility and affordability of these services offered at Government Institutions have strengthened financial protection for families and contributed significantly to improved maternal and neonatal health outcomes. This has been substantiated by National Sample Survey (NSSO 80" Round) which states that the average out-of-pocket expenditure per delivery in Government hospitals is only Rs.1,364/-, compared to Rs.63,473/- in private hospitals. Government hospitals serve

as the primary safeguard against major out-of-pocket healthcare expenditure and the high costs associated with diagnostics and referrals.

motherhood through the Thaimaaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam (Smitompedr srhies Gonr§lnb Hib).

APPENDIX NOTIFICATION-I Jawalagiri — Ulibanda — Thaggatti Elephant Corridor

WHEREAS, the Government of Tamil Nadu is deeply committed to the conservation of Asiatic Elephants and intends to notify elephant corridors, so as to ensure the unobstructed movement of Asian Elephants (Elephas maximus), long-term survival of the species and to mitigate human-wildlife conflict;

AND WHEREAS a Committee has been constituted by the Government vide G.O. (D) No. 296, Environment, Climate Change and Forests (FR.5) Department, dated 26.12.2022, to identify and delineate the corridors and the Committee has submitted its report to the Government through the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests and Chief Wildlife Warden of the State;

AND WHEREAS for the aforesaid purposes, the Government of Tamil Nadu after careful consideration of the said reports have decided to notify the areas mentioned in the Schedule below as Jawalagiri - Ulibanda - Thaggatti Elephant Corridor with effect from the date of publication of this notification.

THE SCHEDULE

I. Name of the Elephant Corridor: Jawalagiri - Ulibanda — Thaggatti II. Description of the Elephant Corridor:

This corridor starts and ends in Ulibanda Reserve Forest of Cauvery South Wildlife Sanctuary by connecting two large habitats i.e. Jawalagiri Reserve Forest in Cauvery North Wildlife Sanctuary and Thaggatty Reserve Forest in Cauvery South Wildlife Sanctuary. The length of the elephant corridor is 18.5 km and the width ranges from 0.73 km to 3.20 km over an extent 3241.53 hectare. It is regular elephant movement along the Madeshvara halla stream (Madeswaran koivai) which connects above two large habitats. Subsequently elephants enter the Thaggatty Reserve Forest and further to Anchetty Reserve Forest.

Devotimaduvu hall, Javugu halla, Rangana Halla, Ichimaduvu Halla, Madesvara halla are the major valley/streams in the Ulibanda Reserve Forest and it further runs up to River Cauvery. This corridor will enable the Trans-Cauvery migration of elephants and other large mammals between the states of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. There is no Bottleneck located in this corridor. The above Reserve Forests, namely Ulibanda and Thaggatty forms part of Cauvery South Wildlife Sanctuary which was notified during 2022 and Jawalagiri Reserve Forest is part of the Cauvery North Wildlife Sanctuary, which was declared in the year 2014.

88. Fisheries and Fishermen Welfare

Inland fisheries and aquaculture have emerged as

vital pillars of Tamil Nadu's rural economy, contributing

significantly to food security, nutritional well-being,

employment generation and sustainable livelihoods.

The State is endowed with an extensive network of inland

water resources, covering about 3.85 lakh hectares,

offering immense potential for fisheries development and

enhancing the livelihoods of thousands of rural families.

i. Enhancement of inland fish production in Rural

Development and Panchayat Raj Department

tanks in Tamil Nadu through fish seed stocking

Tamil Nadu has 21,608 tanks under the control of

the Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Department.

85

With the objective of increasing inland fish production and

enhancing fish productivity in these water bodies, quality

fish fingerlings will be stocked at the rate of 2,000

fingerlings per hectare in 5,000 hectares at a cost of

Rs.75 lakh. This initiative will ensure the availability of

affordable, high-quality protein-rich food for rural

communities.

ii. Promotion of Fish Culture in Multipurpose Farm

Ponds in Tamil Nadu

To encourage fish farmers to undertake fish culture

in farm ponds, subsidy assistance will be provided for the

purchase of essential inputs such as fish fingerlings and

feed for 200 farm ponds. This initiative will improve the

livelihoods of fish farmers while ensuring the availability

of protein-rich food for rural communities. The scheme

will be implemented in selected districts at an estimated

cost of Rs.80 lakh.

89. Rural Development

I. Rural Employment Guarantee and Livelihood

Mission

Under the Rural Employment Guarantee and

Livelihood Mission – Tamil Nadu, planned interventions

86

and water conservation. In addition, agriculture and allied

activities such as drought-proofing, land development,

desilting of supply channels and irrigation canals, and

restoration of traditional water bodies are being carried

out to improve groundwater recharge and soil moisture.

To strengthen connectivity between farmers and

markets in rural areas and facilitate the transportation of

agricultural produce, single-layer gravel roads are being

laid to unconnected Adi Dravidar habitations, tribal

settlements, and hilly areas. During 2026–27, 12,000

works including farm ponds, new ponds, percolation

ponds, water recharge trenches, water recharge shafts,

recharge wells, nurseries, tree planting, earthen bunds

and stone bunds will be taken up at an estimated cost of

Rs.1,500 crore.
